newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's ruling PP at odds with Basque allies.
newsitem.headline: Spain's ruling PP at odds with Basque allies.

text.p: New strains emerged on Monday between Spain's ruling party and its Basque nationalist allies over the conflict with separatist ETA guerrillas, jeopardising their fragile partnership.

Basque regional government President Jose Antonio Ardanza said he would boycott a debate on Tuesday between regional heads and Popular Party (PP) Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar after the PP and Basque nationalists traded insults at the weekend.

Ardanza's Basque National Party (PNV) is the leading political force in the Basque region and supports the government in parliament. The PP, backed by Catalan and Canary Islands parties, can nevertheless muster a majority without the PNV vote.

The allies have increasingly clashed in public over how to resolve the 29-year-long conflict with ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom). The growing tension coincides with an escalation of violence by ETA this year.
The latest row was prompted by an interview with PNV leader Xabier Arzalluz on Friday in the influential French daily newspaper Le Monde.
Arzalluz said Aznar had surrounded himself with hardline rightists who were behind the government's firm refusal to negotiate with the ETA.

"I believe he has people around him who would make your (far-rightist politician Jean-Marie) Le Pen look like a democrat and for whom it would be humiliating for the state to be unable to settle the problem other than through police force," he said.
Carlos Iturgaiz, the PP's leader in the Basque region, responded by saying Arzalluz was "going senile".
The PNV spokesman in Spain's national parliament, Inaki Anasagasti, then insisted Iturgaiz retract the remark, saying he could not support a government that insulted his leader.
"If Mr. Iturguiz does not rectify his words, we will act accordingly," Anasagasti told reporters on Monday.
The PNV asked the government last month to negotiate with the ETA, but Aznar insisted the rebels must first renounce violence.

The PNV and the PP have also parted ways on where ETA prisoners should serve out their terms. The PNV supports a demand by ETA that more than 500 of its prisoners dispersed across the country be moved to jails in the Basque region.
The government rejects any blanket transfer of prisoners, but says it is willing to consider moving prisoners on a case by case basis.
The PNV has criticised Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja for refusing to meet a delegation of Basque parliamentarians pressing for a transfer of prisoners.
Arzalluz told Le Monde that Mayor Oreja did not understand the prisoner issue. Oreja retorted that the government would not be forced into negotiations.
Arzalluz, in the Le Monde interview, reminded Aznar that the conditions for PNV support for the government were that it help complete a devolution of power to the Basque region's government.
"If (Aznar) does not abide by the rules of the game, we'll drop him. And I am not sure that it would be in his interest," Arzalluz said.

Ardanza said on Monday he would boycotting the forum to debating relations between the autonomous regions and the central government in Madrid because the transfer of powers to the Basque government under the PP had not been sufficient.
